pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large numbers — rounding, comparing, ordering, and interpreting real figures (populations, distances, prices) — choosing and justifying a place-value strategy. Applying, not learning, the four-digit toolkit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 10,000] and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding to assess reasonableness, and multi-step contexts.
• Operational details — Pose rich, often multi-step and real-context problems that reward rounding for estimation, comparing/ordering, and flexible partitioning. Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require an explanation of WHY the chosen strategy fits. Emphasise using rounding to check reasonableness and choosing the right degree of accuracy.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): solves a one-step problem (round/compare) with a model. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): solves multi-step place-value problems in context and explains the strategy. Tier C (age 9, extending): selects appropriate accuracy, uses rounding to justify reasonableness, and reasons flexibly with large numbers.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, often multi-step problems (populations, distances, money) that genuinely reward place-value strategies.
Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require justification of the chosen strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and to check the reasonableness of answers.
Teach choosing an appropriate degree of accuracy for the context.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) so strategy selection becomes deliberate.
keyRepresentations: Bar model for multi-step problem structure
Real data sets (populations, distances) as problem material
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a memorised procedure without checking it fits the problem.
Rounding at the wrong stage or to an unhelpful accuracy.
Comparing/ordering errors carried into problem contexts (multi-zero, mixed length).
Not sense-checking an answer against an estimate.
Losing place-value meaning when numbers get large or contextual.

learn.summary: Ages 8-9 applied place-value problem-solving: children choose and justify a place-value strategy (rounding, comparing, ordering, flexible partitioning) to solve rich, multi-step, real-context problems with increasingly large numbers (populations, distances, prices). This is a META topic — the learning target is deliberate strategy selection and using rounding to check reasonableness, not first-time acquisition of the four-digit toolkit.

activities.title: The large-number problem studio
feedback: Name the strategy the child used ('you ordered first, then rounded to estimate') so the choice becomes explicit and reusable.
After the exact answer, show it next to the child's estimate and ask whether the estimate was close enough for the purpose — reinforcing estimation as a reasonableness check.
If the child reached for a procedure that didn't fit, prompt: 'What is the problem actually asking you to find — a comparison, an order, or an estimate?'
activities.rationale: A META problem-solving objective is served by giving children the full toolkit and making them select among tools, so strategy choice and justification are rehearsed rather than a single procedure drilled. Modelling with number lines, bar models and charts and requiring justification reflects recommended place-value pedagogy.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Read a real-context problem such as: four cities have populations 53,847, 48,206, 51,330 and 49,975 — order them from largest to smallest and estimate the total.

Choose which place-value tool fits the task before computing: a number line (for rounding/estimating), an ordering rail (for comparing/ordering), a bar model (for multi-step structure) or a place-value chart (for partitioning).
Act with the chosen tool — e.g. place each population on the ordering rail, then round each to the nearest thousand on the number line and add the rounded values to estimate the total.
State aloud or in writing WHY that tool fit this problem, referencing place value.
Compute the exact answer and compare it against your rounded estimate to check reasonableness.
activities.intendedInsight: The right place-value move depends on what the problem asks; rounding gives a fast estimate that you can use to sense-check an exact answer.

activities.title: Mixed problem set with strategy matching
feedback: For a wrong 'best estimate' choice, place the candidate estimates and the exact figure on a number line to show which is nearer.
For comparison/ordering slips, draw attention to digit place (especially multi-zero numbers and numbers of mixed length).
Confirm when an estimate correctly predicted the size of the exact answer.
activities.rationale: Assessment-style items give varied practice and surface strategy-selection and comparison errors, though a fixed item set scaffolds strategy choice less richly than an open toolkit bench — so it works best as practice alongside the studio.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Work through varied items: multi-step word problems, 'which is larger / best estimate' choices, estimate-then-check tasks, and fill-in-the-blank computations.
For each item, match the problem to the place-value strategy that fits it (round, compare, order, partition) before solving.
Estimate first using rounding, then compute and confirm the estimate was reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Different problem shapes call for different place-value moves; recognising the shape is the first step to solving it.

activities.title: 'How did you decide?' strategy dialogue
feedback: Probe with: 'How did you decide what amount to round to for this puzzle?'
Probe with: 'When would you actually need the exact figure rather than a rounded estimate?'
Probe with: 'Would "about 30" be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? When might that be fine, and when would you need the exact 27 — for example, when handing out one book each?'
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning externalises reasoning and elicits justification, which suits a META topic focused on metacognitive strategy choice; it supplements rather than replaces varied practice.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a real-figure puzzle posed by a partner or teacher (e.g. 'about how many people live in these two towns together?').
Explain which place-value move you chose and why — did you round, compare, or order, and to what accuracy?
Answer probing follow-ups about your choice of accuracy.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a strategy out loud makes strategy selection deliberate and reveals whether the degree of rounding fits the purpose.

activities.title: Diagnostic: is 'about 54,000' fair?
feedback: If the child rejects 'about 54,000' only because it isn't 53,847: discuss why headlines round — the estimate carries the useful information; contrast a bill (exactness matters) with a crowd (it doesn't).

If the child treats all roundings as equally good: compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line so the child can see that the nearest-thousand estimate (54,000) is much closer than the nearest-ten-thousand estimate (50,000). Then discuss that both are correct roundings, and which is more useful depends on the purpose.
This probe surfaces reasoning — use it to understand the child's stance on approximation rather than to grade a single calculation.
activities.rationale: The key judgement underlying large-number problem-solving is whether only exact figures count or whether a sensibly-rounded number is valid and purpose-fit; this open probe surfaces that stance and the common myth that rounding is 'cheating'.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Consider: a news report says a football crowd was 'about 54,000'; the exact number counted was 53,847.
Decide whether 'about 54,000' is a fair thing to report or wrong because it isn't exact, and explain how you'd decide when a rounded number is good enough.
Compare candidate estimates against 53,847 — is 'about 54,000' closer than 'about 50,000'? Which would be more useful for a news report, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A sensibly rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer; how much to round depends on the purpose of the number, and closeness can be judged on a number line.

constraints: This is applying the four-digit place-value toolkit, not first teaching it; learners should already round, compare, order and partition four-digit numbers before this work.

Choice/estimate items and fill-in-the-blank practice assess and rehearse strategy recognition but do not by themselves require the child to select a strategy from an open field — pair recognition tasks with open problems where the child must choose the tool.
The diagnostic probe is not scored; it is meant to surface the child's reasoning about approximation, not produce a mark.
Degree of rounding must be tied to purpose: an estimate fit for a crowd figure is not fit for a bill or a small exact count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked example: 53,847→54,000, 48,206→48,000, 51,330→51,000, 49,975→50,000 to the nearest thousand; rounded sum ≈ 203,000; exact sum = 203,358 — consistent, so the estimate is a reasonable check. Ordering 53,847 > 51,330 > 49,975 > 48,206 is correct. (Example figures beyond the original crowd number were added to make the studio task concrete; flag if a different data set is preferred.)

The original 'about 54,000' is the nearest-thousand rounding of 53,847, which is correct; the contrast 'about 50,000' is deliberately a less-close candidate used diagnostically, not an error, and is never presented to the child as a valid answer.

Editor fix (second pass): Activity 3's third probe still cited 'about 54,000', a figure belonging to the Activity 4 crowd diagnostic and absent from the figure-free two-towns dialogue; it was rewritten to ask generically about rounding a small exact count (27 children) so the scenario stays coherent. A previous pass had fixed the parallel exact-figure probe but missed this one.

Source claims for CCSS-M and NCETM were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as confirmed. The DfE Year 4 claim was marked verified in the legacy row but has not been re-checked here.

Legacy artefact rankings and the 'no spatial payoff' dismissal of 3D were removed as catalog ranking rather than established pedagogy; the underlying pedagogical ideas (toolkit bench, varied quiz practice, Socratic dialogue, worked-example reference) are preserved as distinct activities, with medium limitations stated as scoped rather than universal.

probeDeeper: Is 'about 54,000' closer to the real crowd than 'about 50,000'? Which is fairer?
When would you actually NEED the exact 53,847?
How did you decide the nearest thousand was the right amount to round to?
Would 'about 54,000' be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response accepts that rounding is legitimate and useful, that 'about 54,000' fairly stands for 53,847 (nearest thousand), and that HOW MUCH to round depends on the purpose of the number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes only the exact number is ever correct — rounding is 'wrong' or 'cheating'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why headlines round: the estimate carries the useful information. Contrast contexts where exactness matters (a bill) with where it doesn't (a crowd).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rejects 'about 54,000' purely because it isn't 53,847.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts any rounding without judging closeness — 'about 50,000' seems just as fine as 'about 54,000'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line; the nearest-thousand estimate is the fair one. Tie the degree of rounding to the purpose.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats all roundings as equally good, ignoring which is nearer.

responseLevels.gap: Treats only the exact figure as correct, or accepts any rounding without judging closeness.
responseLevels.full: Judges a rounded number as fair or not by its closeness and by the purpose, and explains the choice using place value.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts rounding as valid but cannot yet justify how much to round for a given purpose.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A news report says a football crowd was “about 54,000”. The exact number counted was 53,847. Is “about 54,000” a fair thing to report, or is it wrong because it isn't the exact number? How would you decide when a rounded number is good enough?' Surface the reasoning — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe surfaces the child's stance on approximation: whether only exact figures count as 'right', or whether a sensibly-rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer. That judgement — not a single calculation — is what place-value problem-solving with large numbers rests on.
